edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page; the packet/page id is missing and a bare page number stands in its place.

edits.quote: Problem 3: Take 1 or 2 counters on each turn. Circle every pile where you would rather go second. (piles 1-12)
edits.fix: P3 asks the same question under the same rule for piles 2-5 that P1 already settled (with a different recording format: circling 1st/2nd vs. circling piles). Either drop P1 and let P3 be the entry, or start P3's boxes at 6 so the work is not repeated.

edits.quote: Draw rings around the counters taken on each turn to show every different way the game can go.
edits.fix: Add 'Use one row for each game.' The board is an undivided grid of 6 rows of 4 (and 9 rows of 5 for P10), so a child can ring across rows; also make clear that taking 1 then 2 is a different game from 2 then 1 (answers: 5 games for 4 counters, 8 for 5).

k-1.summary: A strong K-1 sheet: every pile is drawn, the rules {1,2}, {1,2,3}, {1,3} are contrasted on full 1-12 boards, Ben's fixed 'always take 2' strategy gives a genuine trap hunt, and two-pile and game-counting problems carry it well past forty minutes. All answers check (traps at multiples of 3, 4, and even piles; 20 → 1st/2nd/2nd; (1,4) is a second-player win). Only the footer id, the P1/P3 overlap, and one-row-per-game wording in P9 need fixing.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page; the id is missing and a page number stands in its place.

edits.quote: Decide whether each plan below wins every time, whatever the partner does, and circle your answer. ... For a plan that wins every time, explain why it wins whatever the partner does.
edits.fix: Cut the second 'whatever the partner does'; 'For a plan that wins every time, explain why.' says the same thing.

grades-2-3.summary: This band follows the outline closely: children classify piles 1-20 under {1,3,4} (losing at 2, 7, 9, 14, 16), extend to 25/30/37/50, and test named strategies against every reply, with a good mix of correct and flawed plans (Mia and Ana win; Leo, Sam, Kai's greedy play and Theo's copying lose; Zoe's 'leave 7 or 2' wins). P6's surprise that {1,2,4} gives the same losing piles as {1,2}, and the two-pile mirror problem, add real depth. Apart from the footer and one repeated phrase it is ready to print.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page; the id is missing and a page number stands in its place.

grades-4-5.summary: A rich, correctly built sequence: the period-7 pattern for {1,3,4}, seven rules that pair off ({1,2}/{1,2,4}, {1,3}/{1,3,5}, {1,4}/{1,4,6}), greedy play failing except for the odd-move rules, a reverse problem whose last case (3, 5, 8, 10, ...) is impossible because 2 must be a move, two-pile grids leading into mex labels (11,13 losing; 12,18 winning), and {1,6,9} with a real pre-period (it repeats from 10, period 5) before the pigeonhole question. There is more here than three children will finish, and P8 and P9's explanations are steep, but the steep parts are what the outline asks for and the easier problems give an entry. Only the footer needs changing.

overall.strongest: The grades 2-3 and 4-5 sequences are mathematically correct throughout and develop the outline's kernels (backward induction, testing strategies against every reply, rule changes, Grundy labels, eventual periodicity) through well-chosen contrasting cases with no decorative text.
overall.weakest: Small finishing issues: the footer lacks the required id on every page in all three bands, K-1 P3 repeats P1's piles, and the K-1 P9 game-listing board does not say to use one row per game.
